title: Temporal tuning of illuminance and spectrum: Effect of a full-day dynamic lighting pattern on well-being, performance and sleep in simulated office environment
research_question: To assess the effects of a daylong dynamic lighting (DL) pattern with modulations in intensity and spectrum vs. static office lighting (SL) on markers of well-being, cognitive performance, visual experiences, and sleep in a simulated office environment.

participants.description: 21 college students (8 males), average age 21.52 years (SD=2.29, range 19-26), generally healthy, no visual impairments other than corrected myopia/hyperopia, no smoking/medication/drug use, no recent travel/shift-work, habitual sleep 7-9h, BMI <=25, PSQI <=7, non-extreme chronotype, BDI-II <=10.
participants.recruitment: Via advertisements on the local university, followed by online screening questionnaires.

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
Simulated office environment (3.6x3.6x2.8m) without windows, white walls, light blue floor, 4 workstations. Equipped with six ceiling-mounted tuneable-white Philips RC099V luminaires. Ambient temperature controlled at 26°C (daytime) and 25-27°C (evening/night). Two lighting patterns were used:

Dynamic Lighting (DL) Pattern:
- Early morning (~9:00-10:30) & early afternoon (~14:00-15:30): bright cool white light (6500K, 1000 lx at eye, 1650 lx at table, high melanopic EDI).
- Late morning (~10:30-12:00) & middle afternoon (~15:30-17:00): regular office light (4000K, 345 lx at eye, 500 lx at table).
- Lunchtime (~12:00-14:00) & later afternoon (~17:00-18:00): dimmer warm white light (3000K, 160 lx at eye, 300 lx at table).
- After dinner: 3000K, 40 lx at eye, 78 lx at table.
- Rest phase (19:30-23:00): warm dim white lighting (40 lx, 3000K at eye).
- Sleep (23:00-7:00): lights turned off (<5 lx).

Static Lighting (SL) Pattern:
- Daytime working hours (9:00-18:00): 4000K, 500 lx at table (except for 10:30-12:00 & 15:30-16:00, which matched DL).
- Early morning (7:00-9:00) & evening (18:00-23:00): Same as DL pattern.
- Rest phase (19:30-23:00): warm dim white lighting (40 lx, 3000K at eye).
- Sleep (23:00-7:00): lights turned off (<5 lx).

mechanisms: The dynamic changes in human psychological and physiological function over the day, influenced by varying homeostatic sleep pressure and internal circadian rhythm, modulate sensitivity to light, implying that high melanopic EDI exposure is not always beneficial and should be applied selectively during the wake episode.
implementation_implications: A dynamic lighting approach can be a practical strategy to support office workers' daytime well-being and nocturnal sleep.

High melanopic EDI should be selectively applied during the wake episode, considering dynamic changes in human psychological and physiological function, homeostatic sleep pressure, and circadian rhythm.

limitations: The study was conducted in a well-controlled laboratory setting, restricting participants' activities and preventing exposure to natural light, which may limit ecological validity and generalizability to real operational offices.
The sample size (N=21) and limited number of observations per assessment resulted in low statistical power for detecting small effects and investigating inter-individual differences or random slopes.
The experimental design did not allow for disentangling whether the observed time-dependent and metric-dependent effects were caused by changes in illuminance, spectrum, light history, or timing.
Only one specific dynamic lighting pattern was tested, limiting the generalizability of findings to other potential dynamic lighting scenarios.
The melanopic EDI during lunchtime (160 lx at eye level, ~85 melanopic EDI) was lower than recent recommendations (250 melanopic EDI for daytime exposure).

The melanopic EDI during the evening (15 melanopic EDI) was slightly brighter than recent recommendations (<10 melanopic EDI for evening residential environments), which might have tapered potential differences between lighting patterns.
The 48-hour study duration does not allow for investigating whether the observed effects persist or develop over extended exposure durations (weeks or months) in real-life conditions.
